problem: Prior methods that translate navigation commands into linear temporal logic (LTL) cover only a few short formulas and must be retrained with language data from each new environment and its landmarks. Recent LLM-to-code/plan approaches, such as Code-as-Policies and LM-Nav, cannot express or verify many complex temporal constraints: counting visits, ordering, avoidance and reactions.
motivation: LTL has unambiguous semantics, and LTL planners give soundness guarantees. These include detecting unsatisfiable tasks, which makes LTL a good target for long-horizon temporal navigation commands. The key observation is that the temporal structure of a command is independent of the specific landmarks. Translating a 'lifted' command, with landmarks replaced by placeholders, therefore shrinks the output vocabulary and allows training data from many domains to be pooled. Landmark grounding can then be handled separately by LLMs using a semantic map, enabling transfer to unseen environments without retraining.
key_idea: Split language-to-LTL grounding into three LLM modules and then substitute the grounded propositions back into the formula: (1) recognize referring expressions, (2) ground them to semantic-map landmarks by embedding similarity, and (3) translate the placeholder-lifted command into a lifted LTL formula.
insight: Lifting makes the translator environment-agnostic. It transfers zero-shot to 21 unseen OSM cities (81.83% grounded accuracy) and to prior crowd-sourced datasets without fine-tuning. The proposition modules are near-solved (RER 98.01%, REG 98.20%), so the lifted translation is the bottleneck. Ablations across six lifted translators and three holdout types (utterance / formula / type) show clear trade-offs. Fine-tuned LLMs (T5, GPT-3) are best on paraphrase (utterance) holdout but degrade most on unseen formulas and unseen types. Only prompted GPT models reach meaningful type-holdout accuracy, and mainly on short formulas. Type-constrained decoding only marginally helps T5 on utterance holdout but significantly improves formula/type holdout, indicating that many unseen-formula errors are syntax errors. The most common residual error of fine-tuned models is a syntactically valid formula that matches no known template. Generalizing to unseen formula structures therefore remains open.
method: Referring Expression Recognition (RER): GPT-4 is prompted with a task description and few-shot examples to copy exact substrings (noun phrases and proper names) that refer to propositions/landmarks.

Referring Expression Grounding (REG): each RE is matched to a landmark key k in a semantic database D={k:(z,f)} by maximizing cosine similarity between LLM embeddings of the RE and of the landmark's serialized semantic info z (name, street, amenity, etc.); each grounded proposition is bijectively mapped to a placeholder symbol (A, B, ...).

Lifted Translation: the lifted utterance (REs replaced by placeholders) is translated into a prefix-notation lifted LTL formula over a vocabulary of up to 10 operators and 5 propositions. The main model is fine-tuned T5-Base (220M) with type-constrained decoding, which masks grammar-invalid tokens and, above a maximum parse-tree height, allows only propositions. Alternatives evaluated: fine-tuned GPT-3 (davinci-003), prompted GPT-3/GPT-4, and a Seq2Seq Transformer.

Grounding substitution and planning: placeholders are replaced by the grounded proposition IDs to produce the final LTL formula. The AP-MDP planner computes a plan over the semantic map (product MDP with the Büchi automaton) and aborts on unsatisfiable specifications.

Lifted dataset: 1,156 collected English commands over 15 robotics specification patterns (Menghi et al.), expanded to 47 formula templates with 1-5 propositions. Proposition permutation yields 2,125 unique formulas and 49,655 utterances.

Grounded OSM dataset: GPT-4 paraphrases OpenStreetMap landmark entries into diverse REs, which are substituted into 100 sampled lifted utterances per city for 21 cities (2,100 utterances). Five generalization tests are formalized: paraphrasing, substitution, vocabulary shift, unseen formulas, and unseen template instances.

setting.backbone: GPT-4 (frozen, prompted) for RER + LLM text embeddings (frozen) for REG + T5-Base (fine-tuned, with type-constrained decoding) for lifted translation
setting.training_data: Lifted translator trained on the authors' lifted dataset: 49,655 utterances / 2,125 unique LTL formulas / 47 templates, from 1,156 collected commands with permutation augmentation. For the robot demo, further fine-tuned on 120,000 lifted utterance-formula pairs composed via conjunction/disjunction. No environment-specific language data.
setting.observation: natural-language command + text-labeled semantic map / landmark database (no visual perception in grounding); robot state/position
setting.action_space: outputs an LTL formula; the AP-MDP planner executes primitive moves between neighboring semantic-map nodes (Spot GraphNav graph)
setting.simulator: none (language evaluation on OpenStreetMap landmark databases); real world for the robot demo
setting.privileged: Semantic database of all landmarks with textual attributes and proposition truth functions (pre-built semantic map, e.g. OSM or a Spot GraphNav map) + robot state; pre-mapped environment

numbers_note: This is not a standard embodied-navigation benchmark paper: all metrics are language-to-LTL translation/grounding accuracies, plus a real-robot count. The lifted-translation comparison of six models (fine-tuned T5 ± TCD, fine-tuned GPT-3, prompted GPT-3/GPT-4, Seq2Seq) over utterance/formula/type holdouts is shown only in Fig. 3a and appendix figures, with no printed numbers. The full-system comparison against CopyNet and Prompt GPT-4 on the 21-city OSM data is in Fig. 3b only; only Lang2LTL's 81.83% appears in the text. Prompt GPT-4 was evaluated on a smaller subset. The appendix tables list 58 robot commands (52 correct, 6 OOD failures).
results: Lang2LTL reaches 81.83% grounded LTL translation accuracy on 21 unseen OpenStreetMap cities, beating a retrained CopyNet (Berg et al. 2020) and an end-to-end Prompt GPT-4 baseline (Fig. 3b), with RER/REG module accuracies of 98.01%/98.20%. Zero-shot, it gets 49.40% on Berg et al.'s crowd-sourced OSM data, exceeding in-domain-trained CopyNet (45.91%), and 78.28% on CleanUp World, versus 2.57% for zero-shot CopyNet (in-domain RNN-Attn: 95.51%). On a Spot robot in two indoor environments, it correctly handled 52 commands, including 12 unsatisfiable ones it aborted correctly, versus 23/52 for Code-as-Policies.
limitations: The lifted translator overfits training utterance structures: it fails on unseen compositional patterns (OOD commands in the robot demo) and generalizes poorly to unseen formula skeletons and template types.

Only noun phrases and proper names are handled as referring expressions: no pronouns or coreference, and spatial-relation REs are handled only partially. Duplicate landmarks with identical semantics (e.g., two Starbucks) are resolved at random.
It requires a pre-built, text-labeled semantic map and known robot state, with no visual perception. Evaluation is of formula accuracy rather than embodied navigation success on standard benchmarks.
